tone_statements.quote: Kadu language are certainly tonal; SCHADEBERG (1994) and REH (1994) assume two tones, but MATSUSHITA (1984) posits three for Kadu(gli) and this is also given for Kanga by Kuwa (1994). readall_conflicts: No placement conflict, since no source states a stress placement for Tumtum. There is a difference of characterisation at the Kadu group level between the one work opened in full here, Schadeberg 1994 ('all Kadu languages are almost certainly tone languages', two tones + downstep, stress never mentioned), and the Google-snippet-only Stevenson 1956-57 statement already logged in 'dynamic accent (stress) plays a greater role than syllable pitch, but most languages have some lexical tone doublets'), which was illustrated from Katcha/Krongo/Kamdang rather than Tumtum. Seligmann 1910-11 (opened earlier, scanned) writes stress ticks on Tumtum forms in a wordlist without any statement of where stress falls. None of the three is Tumtum-specific on stress, and none gives a rule.

sources.note: First published Tumtum data (Tumtum column of a seven-dialect wordlist plus sentences). sources.note: No phonology of Tumtum. Footnote 1 only normalises the sources' tone marking ('high tone is represented only on the first vowel of a long vowel; low tone is not explicitly represented'). Useful negative evidence on the state of documentation: 'Krongo, Katcha and Kadugli are the only languages for which there is sufficient information.. Limited data.. from Seligmann (1910-11) and Meinhof (1916-17) for Tumtum' and 'both Seligmann (1910-11) and Meinhof (1916-17) give verbal agreement forms for Tumtum that match all these others'.

sources.note: 55 segments; the inventory includes two tonemes, MODIFIER LETTER HIGH TONE BAR and MODIFIER LETTER LOW TONE BAR (i.e. a two-level tone system), no stress; this is a database encoding of Schadeberg 1994's H-marked/L-unmarked transcription, not an independent statement - the first-hand (group-level) tone statement remains Schadeberg 1994: 18, already held by the project as read.

sources.note: Sec. 3 Phonology, 'a) Tones': all Kadu languages are tonal; Schadeberg (1994) and Reh (1994) assume two tones, Matsushita (1984) posits three for Kadugli and Kuwa (1994) three for Kanga; 'the most common system, though, appears to be two tones plus downstep', areally common in the Nuba Mountains; 'b) Orthographic conventions': no Kadu orthography marks tone (under consideration, Hall 2004).
